data.title: Pityriasis alba — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis alba** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis alba (PA)?**
- Common benign condition of children and adolescents (3–16 y) with ill-defined, slightly scaly hypopigmented patches on the face (cheeks), sometimes neck, upper arms; low-grade eczematous dermatitis — minor criterion of atopic dermatitis
- More noticeable in darker skin and after summer (surrounding skin tans)

**Q2. Clinical stages.**
- Initially mildly erythematous with slightly raised border → hypopigmented patch with fine branny scale → smooth hypopigmented patch
- Asymptomatic or mild itch; 1–4 cm, multiple; extensive PA on trunk (variant) in adults

**Q3. Aetiology.**
- Atopy, xerosis, sun exposure (UV), frequent bathing/soaps, possibly Malassezia and low serum copper; post-inflammatory hypopigmentation from reduced melanosome transfer due to inflammation/oedema

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Non-specific mild spongiotic dermatitis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, reduced melanin, normal or slightly reduced melanocytes

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Pityriasis versicolor (KOH positive, upper trunk), vitiligo (chalk-white, sharp, Wood's bright), indeterminate leprosy (sensation, nerve), nevus depigmentosus (congenital stable), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, seborrhoeic dermatitis, hypopigmented MF (persistent trunk patches in adults), progressive macular hypomelanosis, tinea faciei

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance — self-limiting (months to years), repigments
- Emollients, gentle soap substitute, sunscreen to reduce contrast
- Mild topical steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) short course or calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) for scaly/inflamed patches; calcitriol; excimer laser for persistent extensive PA

**Q7. What is the association between PA and atopic dermatitis?**
- PA is a minor criterion in Hanifin and Rajka criteria; children with AD and xerosis get PA more frequently, especially after sun exposure and frequent bathing; treating xerosis prevents it

**Q8. What is extensive pityriasis alba?**
- Widespread non-scaly hypopigmented macules on trunk/limbs in adults without atopy — overlaps with progressive macular hypomelanosis; poor response to topical agents; NB-UVB/PUVA helps

**Q9. What is progressive macular hypomelanosis?**
- Ill-defined, non-scaly, hypopigmented coalescing macules on the trunk of young adults (especially darker skin); associated with Cutibacterium acnes (red follicular fluorescence on Wood's lamp); treated with benzoyl peroxide + clindamycin and NB-UVB, doxycycline

## Quick spotter facts
- Ill-defined scaly hypopigmented cheek patches in atopic child — pityriasis alba
- Check sensation to exclude leprosy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypopigmentation). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
